source: Plaut, Nguyen, Trinh (2025, TMLR) Probabilities of Chat LLMs Are Miscalibrated but Still Predict Correctness on Multiple-Choice Q&A
finding: Standard practice for multiple choice: take the probability of each option letter, renormalize to sum to 1, use the maximum (MSP). MSP is miscalibrated but ranks right answers above wrong ones. Gap 1 and 3: this studies the renormalised max, not raw versus renormalised.
numbers: 15 chat LLMs, 5 datasets, 280 AUROC points; MSP AUROC beat chance (p<1e-4) in 245 of 280, and 196 of 200 without Falcon and Llama 2. Q&A accuracy explains R2=0.94 of MSP AUROC; accuracy explains only R2=0.07 (p=0.33) of calibration error. Examples (accuracy / MSP AUROC): Llama 3.1 70B 80.6/83.4; GPT-3.5 Turbo 67.5/76.1; Falcon 7B 30.1/52.0.
quote: We first compute the probability that the LLM assigns to each answer token and renormalize those probabilities to sum to 1.
limits: Letter-token probabilities only; no comparison against un-normalised scores or independent per-option elicitation. Per-dataset calibration error x100: ARC-C 13.6, HellaSwag 19.6, MMLU 24.1, TruthfulQA 30.6, WinoGrande 24.2.
agent_relevance: Forced sum-to-one over letters is the default and gives a usable confidence (max prob), but not a calibrated one. Use it as a ranking signal for abstain or re-check, not as a literal probability.

source: Plaut et al. (2025) Section 6: Q&A with abstention
finding: Using the renormalised MSP as a threshold, abstaining when it is low improved the score for most models, with only 20 labelled questions per dataset to set the threshold.
numbers: Scoring: +1 correct, 0 abstain, -1 (balanced) or -2 (conservative) per wrong answer; threshold from k=20 questions. MSP abstention beat never abstaining for most of the 15 models; table cells came out garbled in text extraction so per-model values are not recorded.
limits: Single pass, so no extra tokens. Not compared against resampling at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: A cheap stop-or-escalate signal: if the renormalised max prob is low, do not answer or spend more compute. Needs a small labelled set to choose the threshold.

source: Poppi, Yong et al. (2025, v2 2026) Improving LLM First-Token Predictions in Multiple-Choice QA via Output Prefilling
finding: The first-token distribution often puts mass on tokens that are not valid options (misalignment, preamble). Prefilling a prefix such as 'The correct option is:' fixes the format and improves accuracy and calibration. This is the practical form of a forced partition: all mass falls on the exclusive options.
numbers: Accuracy gain vs plain first-token probability: Gemma-2-9B +25.9, Gemma-7B +14.9, Zephyr-7B +3.4, Llama-3.1-8B +6.0, Phi-4-14B +7.3. ACE Llama-3.1-8B MMLU 0.206 to 0.129, OpenBookQA 0.444 to 0.252; Phi-4 OpenBookQA 0.340 to 0.272. Valid-token rate up over 60 points for Gemma-2-9B and Llama-3.1-8B.
quote: prefilling substantially improves accuracy, calibration, and output consistency across a broad set of LLMs and MCQA benchmarks
limits: Open-weight 7B-14B models, first-token scoring; gain comes mostly from format validity, not coherence as such. Not tested at equal tokens against resampling.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct LLM evidence for gap 1: constraining probability mass to the exclusive options helps calibration and accuracy. The cause is validity of the support, which a sum-to-one guardrail enforces.

source: Zheng et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors (PriDe)
finding: LLMs put prior mass on option-ID tokens (A/B/C/D). Moving the gold answer to a fixed position changes accuracy a lot. PriDe estimates the ID prior on a few samples and divides it out of the option distribution, which usually raises accuracy.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks. gpt-3.5-turbo MMLU 0-shot: gold at D drops accuracy 67.2 to 60.9 (-6.3). llama-30b gold at A gains +15.2 and reaches 68.2 vs gpt-3.5 65.3 (default 53.1 vs 67.2). PriDe with 5 percent of samples for prior estimation matches or beats cyclic permutation at lower cost.
limits: Authors say PriDe targets selection bias, not accuracy; accuracy gain is a side effect and degrades slightly under big domain shift (STEM/Humanities to ARC).
agent_relevance: Renormalising alone leaves a systematic bias in which exclusive option gets the mass. Pair the guardrail with option-order shuffling or a prior correction. Gap 2 in part: more than plain renormalisation helps, via prior correction rather than coherence projection.

source: Zhao, Wallace, Feng, Klein, Singh (2021, ICML) Calibrate Before Use
finding: Few-shot prompting is biased by majority label, recency and common tokens. Contextual calibration: renormalise label probabilities to one, then rescale by the probabilities given a content-free input such as N/A. Fixes much of the bias without labelled data.
numbers: GPT-3 average and worst-case accuracy improved by up to 30.0 points absolute; GPT-3 2.7B with calibration sometimes beat uncalibrated 175B by up to 19.3 points; variance across training-example sets reduced in most cases.
limits: 2021 GPT-3 base models; classification plus some generation tasks; calibration vector fitted per prompt on content-free inputs. Not a coherence method.
agent_relevance: Renormalising over option labels is the baseline and a diagonal rescaling adds measured accuracy. Supports gap 2: simple per-label rescaling is cheap and works.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: With visible lettered options, large models are well calibrated on multiple choice (option probabilities behave like a partition). Calibration improves with size and with 5-shot. RLHF policies look miscalibrated but a temperature fix repairs much of it.
numbers: Models up to 52B; BIG-Bench, MMLU, TruthfulQA with visible choices; calibration error falls with parameters (figures only; no headline number extracted).
quote: when we use a format with visible lettered answer options, large models are very well calibrated on diverse multiple choice questions
limits: Calibration depends on format; weaker in other formats. 2022 Anthropic base models, not current reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Format matters for coherence. Show all exclusive options at once so the model compares them; expect temperature to matter for RLHF models.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Section 3.1: replacing an option with none of the above
finding: Gap 4. In LLMs an explicit residual option does not behave like the human unpacking effect. Models are biased against choosing none of the above, and accuracy and calibration fall a lot when one option is replaced by it.
numbers: MMLU: replacing option (D) with none of the above lowers accuracy very significantly (Figure 7, 52B, 0-shot and 5-shot) and makes calibration of the (D) option much worse. 20-shot did not fix it.
quote: It seems that even the 52B model is biased against using the none of the above option
limits: 2022 models, MMLU replacement design (some items become ill-posed). Not a test of Tversky and Koehler unpacking: it tests residual usage, not whether unpacked parts sum above the packed whole.
agent_relevance: The residual slot is under-used, so mass that belongs to other is pushed onto named options and the named sum runs too high. A guardrail must force residual mass explicitly (ask for it, or check the named sum against 1) rather than rely on the model picking it.

source: Tian et al. (2023, EMNLP) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: For RLHF models, verbalised probabilities are better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for the top-k guesses with a probability each, in one response, improves calibration on hard sets as k grows. The k guesses act as a partition of the answer space.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo ECE, Verb. 1S top-1/top-2/top-4: TruthfulQA 0.389/0.361/0.203; TriviaQA 0.068/0.050/0.054; SciQ 0.234/0.132/0.065. Label-prob ECE on TruthfulQA 0.451. Overall ECE cut by a relative 50 percent across ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude.
quote: directly verbalizing a probability yields significantly better-calibrated confidence estimates
limits: Free-form answers scored on the top guess. Not monotone on easy sets. The sum of the k probabilities is not checked.
agent_relevance: Asking for several exclusive answers with probabilities gives a partition-like distribution cheaply. Gap 1: supportive but not an equal-token test against independent per-option judging.

source: Xiong et al. (2024, ICLR) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Verbalised confidence is overconfident. Human-inspired prompts (CoT, Top-K, Self-Probing) lower ECE; sample consistency helps failure prediction. Top-K best for GPT-3.5, Self-Probing most consistent for GPT-4. No single strategy wins.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 5 dataset types. White-box vs black-box AUROC gap narrow: 0.522 vs 0.605. GPT-3 to GPT-4 about 22.2 percent AUROC gain. Vicuna and GPT-3.5 average ECE above 0.377.
quote: Top-K ... acts as a normalization for the confidence distribution.
limits: ECE falls easily; failure prediction (AUROC) stays weak, especially on professional-knowledge tasks. Effect of CoT on coherence itself not measured.
agent_relevance: Partial for gap 5: reasoning prompts lower overconfidence but do not close the discrimination gap. Whether CoT reduces probability-identity violations is still untested.

source: Robinson and Wingate (2023, ICLR) Leveraging LLMs for Multiple Choice Question Answering
finding: Showing all options and having the model output the option symbol (multiple choice prompt) beats the cloze method, which scores each option separately with ad hoc length normalisation. Strong models with symbol binding ability benefit most.
numbers: 20 datasets: multiple choice prompt beats cloze on all but 4, mean gap 9.7 points, max gap 44; 0.6 below prior SOTA on average and above old SOTA on 9 of 20 (up to 15 points).
limits: Needs models with symbol-binding ability; weak models do better with cloze. Accuracy only, no calibration or sum check.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: joint presentation of exclusive options (one softmax over letters) beats independent per-option scoring, in one forward pass. Cleanest measured case for the partition framing of the guardrail.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Dutch Book Arguments (Vineberg)
finding: Gaps 7 and 10. Pragmatic version (Ramsey, de Finetti) ties credence to betting quotients. Depragmatized versions (Howson and Urbach; Christensen) drop the claim that agents act on credences but still rely on value judgements about bets. The Lewis/Teller diachronic book for conditionalization uses four bets; van Fraassen objects that it assumes the update rule is fixed in advance.
numbers: Four bets priced Pr1(A and E), Pr1(A|E)Pr1(not E), [Pr1(A|E)-Pr2(A)]Pr1(E), Pr2(A). No numeric example given. Hajek's Czech Book cancels the book; avoidable by requiring fair-or-favourable bets.
quote: an agent can always prevent a sure loss by simply refusing to bet
limits: Read via page fetch summary of the first 100000 of 105176 characters.
agent_relevance: For an agent that never bets, the pragmatic argument is weak; the accuracy argument (d12) fits better. The diachronic book supports checking updates against a pre-committed rule, not only one-shot sums.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epistemic Utility Arguments for Probabilism (Pettigrew)
finding: Gap 7. Dominance theorem: with a continuous strictly proper score every non-probabilistic credence function is strongly dominated by a probabilistic one, and no probabilistic one is even weakly dominated. No bettor needed.
numbers: Worked example: credences 0.6 on X and 0.6 on not-X give Brier inaccuracy 0.52 in both worlds; 0.5 and 0.5 give 0.50 in both, so the coherent pair wins everywhere. Objections: different measures give different dominators (Bronfman); Easwaran and Fitelson trick-coin case; Thwarted Accuracy; Carr 2015 on expansions.
limits: Read first 100000 of 140410 characters via page fetch. Holds for strictly proper scores only. Proofs (Joyce 1998, Leitgeb and Pettigrew 2010) not opened.
agent_relevance: Adds a second review for K03. Justifies renormalising over exclusive options as an accuracy move under Brier, with no betting. The guardrail is justified for Brier-type loss, not necessarily for 0-1 accuracy.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Formal Epistemology, sections 2.1-2.2
finding: Dutch books are pragmatic and may show only pragmatic irrationality; Christensen and Vineberg reply. Accuracy arguments (Joyce 1998, 2009) say violators are unnecessarily far from the truth. Carr (2017) criticises the approach. Conditionalization is backed by Teller 1973 and Lewis 1999 (books), Greaves and Wallace 2006 and Leitgeb and Pettigrew 2010 (accuracy).
limits: Summary of first 100000 of 155605 characters. Non-ideal agent objections not covered in this entry.
agent_relevance: The choice of justification (gap 7) stays open; for updates an accuracy route exists (Greaves and Wallace), not only diachronic books.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Section 3.2: True/False and P(True)
finding: Asking about each proposed answer separately (True/False) also gives calibrated P(True), improving with size. Independent judging works, but the multiple choice format needed only relative weights.
numbers: Shown in figures only; no single number extracted.
quote: the model only needs to determine the relative weight for several concrete options
limits: Per-option P(True) values are not forced to sum to 1 in the paper; the sum was not reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the raw sum of independent P(True) over exclusive options is a candidate free uncertainty signal, but nobody here measured it against correctness.

finding: No new primary papers could be opened for gaps 5, 6, 8, 9, 10. The web search budget was exhausted and the arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned rate-limit errors.
limits: This is a search failure, not evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Do not treat gaps 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 as answered; rerun the search later.
